etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pronunciacioun, from Middle French prononciation, pronunciation, from Latin prōnūntiātiō, noun of action from perfect passive participle prōnūntiātus, from verb prōnūntiāre (“proclaim”), from prō- (“for”) + nūntiāre (“announce”). Doublet of pronuntiatio.

definitions.definition: (countable) The formal or informal way in which a word is made to sound when spoken.

quote.citation: 1791, John Walker, A Critical Pronouncing Dictionary […] ‎[2], London: Sold by G. G. J. and J. Robinſon, Paternoſter Row; and T. Cadell, in the Strand, →OCLC, page 211:
quote.text: ☞ This word [earth] is liable to a coarſe vulgar pronunciation, as if written Urth; […]

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The way in which the words of a language are made to sound when speaking.

quote.citation: 1687, Chriſtopher Cooper, “Chap. XIX: Of Barbarous Speaking”, in The Engliſh Teacher, London: John Richardſon, for the Author, pages 77-78; republished Menston: Scolar Press, 1969:
quote.text: He, that would write exactly, muſt avoid a Barbarous Pronunciation, and conſider for facility, or thorow miſtake, many words are not ſounded after the beſt dialect. Such as  […]  Wun, one.

definitions.definition: (countable) The act of pronouncing or uttering a vocable.

quote.citation: 1831, Thomas Oughton, James Thomas Law, Forms of Ecclesiastical Law, page 62:
quote.text: The second part is the sentence, which is the judge's pronunciation upon a cause depending between two in controversy.
